senses.definition: A piece of metal placed in a horse's mouth and connected to the reins to direct the animal.
examples: A horse hates having a bit put in its mouth.

senses.definition: A rotary cutting tool, fitted to a drill, brace, or router, used to bore or drill holes or to remove material from the profile of the workpiece.
examples: router bit
chamfering bit

senses.definition: Applied to a various small units of currency and coins.

subsenses.definition: (dated, British) A coin of a specified value.
examples: a threepenny bit

subsenses.definition: (historical, US and Canada) A unit of currency worth one eighth of a dollar, originally of a Spanish dollar but later also US or Canadian; also, a coin with this value, in particular the silver Spanish real.
examples: A quarter is two bits.

quotes.text: He left after shaking her down for four bits for carrying the bags.

subsenses.definition: (obsolete, US and Canada) A coin of a value similar but not equal to this, in particular the ‘short bit’, i.e. the ten-cent piece or dime.

quotes.text: The smallest coin we had in Canada in early days was a dime, worth ten cents. The Indians called this coin “a Bit”. Our next coin, double in buying power and in size, was a twenty-five cent piece and this the Indians called “Two Bits”.

subsenses.definition: (historical) A unit of currency and coin of the British West Indies worth six black dogs, originally equal to one-eighth of a Spanish dollar but later increasingly debased to one tenth, one eleventh, one twelfth, etc.

quotes.text: I trusted to the Lord to be with me; and at one of our trips to St. Eustatia, a Dutch island, I bought a glass tumbler with my half bit, and when I came to Montserrat I sold it for a bit, or sixpence.

subsenses.definition: (historical) A unit of currency of the Dutch West Indies in the early 20th century, worth one fifth of a cent.

senses.definition: A small amount of something.
examples: There were bits of paper all over the floor.
Does your leg still hurt? —Just a bit now.
I've done my bit; I expect you to do yours.

quotes.text: ‘No,’ said Luke, grinning at her. ‘You're not dull enough! […] What about the kid's clothes? I don't suppose they were anything to write home about, but didn't you keep anything? A bootee or a bit of embroidery or anything at all?’

senses.definition: (informal) Specifically, a small amount of time.
examples: I'll be there in a bit; I need to take care of something first.
He was here just a bit ago, but it looks like he's stepped out.

senses.definition: (informal) A small fraction above a whole number.
examples: The movie lasted for two and a bit hours.

senses.definition: (in the plural, informal, sports) Fractions of a second.
examples: The 400 metres race was won in 47 seconds and bits.

senses.definition: A portion of something.
examples: I'd like a big bit of cake, please.

senses.definition: Somewhat; something, but not very great; also used like jot and whit to express the smallest degree. See also a bit.
examples: Am I bored? Not a bit of it!

quotes.text: My young companion was a bit of a poet.

senses.definition: A replaceable tip for a hand tool or power tool, comprising the portion that drives a fastener.
examples: Near-synonym: driver
driver bit

examples: His bit about video games was not nearly as entertaining as the other segments of his show.

senses.definition: (mathematics, computing) A binary digit, generally represented as a 1 or 0.
(computing) The smallest unit of storage in a digital computer, consisting of a binary digit.
(information theory, cryptography) Any datum that may take on one of exactly two values.
examples: status bits on IRC
permission bits in a file system

senses.definition: (information theory) A unit of measure for information entropy.

quotes.text:
The researchers found that the original texts spanned a variety of entropy values in different languages, reflecting differences in grammar and structure.
But strangely, the difference in entropy between the original, ordered text and the randomly scrambled text was constant across languages. This difference is a way to measure the amount of information encoded in word order, Montemurro says. The amount of information lost when they scrambled the text was about 3.5 bits per word.
